newsitem.title: UK: Abbey Nat sees UK house recovery in '97, no "boom'.
newsitem.headline: Abbey Nat sees UK house recovery in '97, no "boom'.

text.p: Abbey National Plc, one of Britain's biggest mortgage lenders, does not expect a return to the housing market's feast-to-famine cycle of the late 1980s, but sees average house prices rising by seven percent in 1997.
Abbey also forecasts no "significant" increases in interest rates in the foreseeable future -- allowing the fragile recovery in consumer confidence to continue.
"We do not anticipate -- and would not welcome -- a return to the boom-bust cycle of the late 1980s," the bank said.

The trend for price growth next year will vary by region, with the currently less buoyant Midlands and Northern regions enjoying sharper increases in prices as they catch up with Greater London, the southern regions and Wales, it said.
Abbey said the UK housing market "improved significantly" in the second half of 1996 as the volume of property transactions picked up sharply from July.
It expects transactions for the whole of 1996 to be up about 10 percent to about 1.25 million. Next year's total should be around 1.4 million, up by 10 to 12 percent.
"This (1997) will be the highest level since 1990, although this is still some way off from the average 1.6 million transactions experienced before the late '80s boom," it said.
Home-related borrowing activity should also recover in line with increased house buying.

Mortgage lending by banks and building societies is estimated to total 18 billion pounds -- still some 20 billion below the peak levels seen in the late 1980s -- to bring the pool of outstanding borrowings in Britain to 400 billion pounds.
Abbey National sees mortgage lending totalling 20 billion stg a year by 1998. With increased demand a reduction in special offers, cashbacks and discounts is likely.
